summary: A combination of an antidepressant and an antipsychotic used for depression with a lot of anxiety or agitation, or schizophrenia with depression symptoms. It can work, but its side effects and safety warnings are serious, and it is not usually a first choice.
description: Amitriptyline/perphenazine combines a tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline) with an older (first-generation) antipsychotic (perphenazine). It is used when depression comes with a lot of anxiety, agitation, or sleep problems – and sometimes for schizophrenia with depression symptoms. It can be sedating and calming, but it also carries real risks: warnings about suicidal thoughts (especially under 25), movement side effects (stiffness, shaking, restlessness, and lasting involuntary movements called tardive dyskinesia (TD)), dangerous drying effects (constipation, trouble peeing), dizziness or fainting when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), heart rhythm problems, and a boxed warning about a higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. It is not approved for children.
patient_summary: This medicine is a two-in-one: an older antidepressant plus an older antipsychotic. The combination can help when depression is mixed with anxiety or agitation, but the tradeoff is side effects. People often feel calmer and sleepier, but they can also get dry mouth, constipation, dizziness when standing, brain fog, and (from the antipsychotic part) restlessness or stiffness. It has major safety warnings, interacts with many medicines (especially MAOIs and sedatives), and it is generally avoided in older adults.

primary.context: Used for unipolar depression when anxiety and agitation are prominent and a sedating/calming approach is part of the plan.
Used when schizophrenia includes depressive symptoms; dosing is higher and side-effect monitoring becomes even more important.

secondary.context: Targets anxiety symptoms occurring alongside depression, especially when agitation, insomnia, or distress is intense.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Many people feel calmer and sleepier early on. That can help with agitation or trouble sleeping, but it can also cause brain fog and trouble functioning during the day – especially while the dose is being raised.
Dry mouth is common with amitriptyline. It’s annoying, but it also matters medically (teeth/gum issues). Hydration, sugar-free gum/lozenges, and dental care help.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Blood pressure can drop when standing. If you’re getting lightheaded, near-fainting, or falls, that’s a dose-limiting side effect.

Perphenazine can cause movement side effects. A strong inner restlessness (akathisia) can feel like unbearable inner agitation and is sometimes mistaken for worse anxiety – tell your clinician quickly.
These can become serious. If you can’t pee, or you go days without a bowel movement with abdominal pain, treat it as urgent.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal ideation or worsening depression, especially early in treatment or after dose changes
Involuntary movements that can last, called tardive dyskinesia (TD): the risk goes up with how long you take it and the total dose over time
A rare emergency with fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, and unstable heart rate and blood pressure (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS)
Life-threatening arrhythmias or conduction abnormalities, especially with cardiac disease or overdose
Blood problems: a dangerous drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can be fatal; get care for fever, sore throat, or signs of infection
Aspiration pneumonia risk in vulnerable populations due to dysphagia/esophageal dysmotility
Low blood sodium (hyponatremia), especially in older adults (confusion, weakness, falls)
Hyperthermia and impaired temperature regulation (heat intolerance, dehydration risk)

safety.black_box_warning:
Suicidal thoughts in children, teens, and young adults: In short-term studies, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children and teens with depression (MDD) and other mental health conditions. Everyone taking it should be watched closely – especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose changes – for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts, or unusual changes in behavior. This medicine is not approved for children.

Higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis: Older adults with dementia who have psychosis (losing touch with reality) and take antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. This medicine is not approved to treat dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to amitriptyline, perphenazine, or any component of the formulation (cross-sensitivity with other phenothiazines may exist)
Use with or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
CNS depression due to barbiturates, alcohol, opioids, analgesics, or antihistamines
During the acute recovery phase of myocardial infarction (MI)

precautions: Not approved for pediatric use; antidepressant-related suicidality monitoring is still relevant across ages, especially under 25
Avoid in older adults when possible: strong drying effects (dry mouth, constipation, confusion), sleepiness, blood pressure drops when standing, falls, confusion, and risk of low blood sodium
Movement side effects from perphenazine, including lasting ones called tardive dyskinesia (TD): stiffness, shaking, restlessness, abnormal movements that can become permanent
A rare but life-threatening reaction with fever, stiff muscles, confusion, and unstable heart rate and blood pressure (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS)
Heart risks: altered cardiac conduction and arrhythmias can occur; risk is higher with underlying cardiac disease and in overdose
Drying side effects can become dangerous: severe constipation or a blocked bowel, trouble peeing, blurred vision, sudden confusion (delirium)
Mania/hypomania risk: can precipitate mood switching in bipolar-spectrum illness; screen for bipolar disorder before starting
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can contribute to dysphagia/aspiration risk, especially in older adults
Photosensitivity: can increase sensitivity to sun exposure
Surgery: manufacturer recommends discontinuation prior to elective surgery due to interaction/arrhythmia risk; discontinuation must be weighed against relapse/discontinuation risks

interactions.mechanism: Dangerous interaction risk; requires washout period.
interactions.action: Do not use together. Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting amitriptyline/perphenazine, and allow 14 days between stopping this medication and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Alcohol, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, benzodiazepines
interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression: heavy sedation, impaired coordination, accidents, respiratory risk in vulnerable patients.
interactions.action: Avoid or use only with careful clinician review. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

interactions.interactant: Other drying medicines (anticholinergics), e.g., diphenhydramine, many bladder medicines, some antipsychotics/TCAs
interactions.mechanism: Too much drying effect: severe constipation or blocked bowel, trouble peeing, confusion or delirium, blurred vision, overheating.
interactions.action: Keep the number of drying medicines as low as possible. If you are already constipated, having trouble peeing, or confused, this combination is a problem – tell your prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of conduction abnormalities/arrhythmias, especially with cardiac disease or electrolyte issues.
interactions.action: Review full med list for QT risk. Consider ECG monitoring when clinically indicated.

interactions.mechanism: Increased seizure risk in susceptible patients.
interactions.action: Use caution in seizure disorder, brain injury, heavy alcohol use history, or when combining multiple threshold-lowering meds.

interactions.interactant: A body that breaks it down slowly (CYP2D6 poor metabolizer), or medicines that strongly slow its breakdown (CYP2D6 inhibitors)
interactions.mechanism: Higher plasma concentrations at usual doses can raise side-effect risk.
interactions.action: A lower dose and slower dose increases may be used, with close checks on how you are doing.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidal thoughts and worsening mood: watched closely, especially early in treatment and during dose changes; family or caregivers are involved when appropriate
Mental status and alertness: sedation, confusion, delirium risk (especially in older adults or with sedative combinations)
Blood pressure lying and standing: checked for drops when standing and fall risk
EPS: assess every visit; repeat at ~4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk)
Involuntary movements that can last – tardive dyskinesia (TD): checked every visit, with a formal rating scale at least once a year (or every 6 months if high risk)
Weight/BMI: monitor every visit for first 6 months, then quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually when metabolic risk is a concern
Fasting glucose/HbA1c: around 4 months after initiation and then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel: around 4 months after initiation and then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Blood count (CBC): when needed; more often early on if you already have low white blood cells or have had a drop in white blood cells from a medicine
Blood chemistries: electrolytes, renal function, liver function, and TSH as clinically indicated

Prolactin hormone: you will be asked about symptoms at each visit until things are stable; levels are checked if symptoms appear (period changes, sex-drive changes, breast growth in men, milky nipple discharge, sexual problems)
ECG (heart tracing): at the start and when needed in older adults and people who already have heart disease or heart-rhythm risk
Blood sodium: in people at risk (especially older adults) when needed; watch for signs of low sodium (confusion, weakness, falls)
Body temperature control: watch the risk with heat, dehydration, hard exercise, and taking several drying medicines
Eye effects: eye exams when needed; the risk is considered with long-term use of this type of antipsychotic (phenothiazine) and in people with diabetes or vision concerns
Therapeutic drug monitoring (optional/selected cases): trough levels can help confirm adherence; dosing should still be based on clinical response and tolerability

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies did not show harm. Decisions should be based on the risks of each of the two medicines, how severe the illness is, and safer options when available.
special_populations.lactation: Amitriptyline and perphenazine are present in breast milk. Breastfeeding is not recommended by the manufacturer; if considered, it requires careful clinician oversight and infant monitoring.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for children. Antidepressants carry a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults; this combination is not FDA-approved for children.
special_populations.geriatric: Generally avoided. Amitriptyline has strong drying effects (dry mouth, constipation, trouble peeing, confusion) and can cause sleepiness and dizziness when standing up. Perphenazine (an antipsychotic) may be unsafe for older adults because of the risk of stroke, memory and thinking decline, and death (especially in dementia-related psychosis). Falls, sudden confusion (delirium), and low blood sodium are key concerns.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Use caution with kidney problems. Dosing is usually guided by the two individual medicines and by how well you tolerate it.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use caution, because the body may clear it more slowly and blood levels may be higher. A careful approach uses lower starting and ongoing doses, raised slowly; some experts suggest cutting the amitriptyline dose a lot and keeping the maximum lower with liver problems.

dosing.titration: Dosing is typically divided across the day (2 to 4 doses). Your prescriber adjusts based on response and tolerability, with a firm ceiling on the daily maximum for both components.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Don’t stop this medication abruptly unless a clinician tells you to for a safety emergency. Both components can cause rebound and withdrawal-style symptoms. The safer approach is usually a gradual taper, tailored to how long you’ve been on it, your dose, and your symptom history.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Amitriptyline/perphenazine is used in psychiatry for people who aren’t just “sad” or “anxious,” but wired-up, agitated, and struggling to function—where a medication that calms the nervous system and treats depression at the same time is being considered. It’s not approved for pediatric use.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Unipolar Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)} with moderate to severe anxiety and/or agitation
Depression with prominent anxiety, insomnia, or agitation where sedation is part of the clinical goal
{link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia} with depressive symptoms

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: My brain finally stopped sprinting—like the buzzing got turned down.
I felt calmer, but also kind of heavy and sleepy.
It helped me slow down at night, but mornings were rough at first.
The edge came off first, then my mood started lifting later.
I wasn’t spiraling as hard. Still depressed, but less panicky.
It didn’t fix everything overnight, but I felt more stable.
items.note: Antidepressant benefits usually build over days to weeks. The calming/sedating effect can show up earlier.

quotes: Dry mouth like the Sahara. I carried water everywhere.
Constipation was the worst part for me—had to actively manage it.
Blurred vision and trouble peeing freaked me out.
items.note: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and urinary retention can be major limiting side effects, especially with amitriptyline.

items.category: Movement Side Effects (from the antipsychotic part)
quotes: I felt restless, like I couldn’t sit still.
My body felt stiff and weird, like my muscles didn’t cooperate.
I got this uncomfortable inner jitter that wasn’t anxiety—different feeling.
items.note: Akathisia (inner restlessness), stiffness, tremor, and other EPS can happen and can feel miserable—report it fast.

quotes: If I stood up too fast, I’d see stars.
I had to move slower—especially in the morning.
I felt wobbly for the first couple of weeks.
items.note: Orthostatic hypotension (BP drop when standing) is a known risk with both components and increases fall risk.

sections.intro: Real talk: this is an “older school” combo med, and people often notice it in their body quickly—sometimes in helpful ways, sometimes in annoying ways.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: This combo can calm agitation and help sleep earlier than it improves depression. Think: calming first, mood next.
key_points: First few doses: Sedation/calm can show up early (especially if you’re sensitive)
First 1-2 weeks: Anxiety/agitation may soften as the nervous system settles
2-6+ weeks: Antidepressant effect is more likely to be noticeable and consistent
Day-to-day duration: Effects depend on dose timing (often divided doses) and how sedating it is for you
If you miss doses or stop abruptly: You can get rebound symptoms or a discontinuation syndrome

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: This medication is used when the clinical target is a specific cluster: depression plus significant anxiety/agitation (sometimes with insomnia). The “win” looks like fewer spirals, less agitation, improved sleep, and better day-to-day function—without unacceptable side effects like severe dizziness, heart rhythm issues, or movement symptoms.
sections.metric: Clinical improvement in depression with anxiety/agitation
sections.clinical_details: Because this is a combination product with two older agents (a tricyclic antidepressant and a typical antipsychotic), response is usually evaluated symptom-by-symptom: mood, anxiety, agitation, sleep, and functional impairment. Dose changes are typically based on both benefit and tolerability, and many patients stop or switch if anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, or EPS show up.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This medicine has boxed warnings about suicidal thoughts (especially under 25) and a higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box:
Suicidal thoughts in children, teens, and young adults: In short-term studies, antidepressants raised the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children and teens with depression (MDD) and other mental health conditions. Everyone taking it should be watched closely – especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose changes – for worsening mood, suicidal thoughts, or unusual changes in behavior. This medicine is not approved for children.

Higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis: Older adults with dementia who have psychosis (losing touch with reality) and take antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. This medicine is not approved to treat dementia-related psychosis.
other: Not approved for pediatric use; antidepressant-related suicidality monitoring is still relevant across ages, especially under 25
Avoid in older adults when possible: high anticholinergic burden, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, falls, confusion, and hyponatremia risk
EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk from perphenazine (stiffness, tremor, restlessness, abnormal movements that can become persistent)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is rare but life-threatening: fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Heart risks: altered cardiac conduction and arrhythmias can occur; risk is higher with underlying cardiac disease and in overdose
Anticholinergic effects can become dangerous: severe constipation/ileus, urinary retention, blurred vision, delirium
Mania/hypomania risk: can precipitate mood switching in bipolar-spectrum illness; screen for bipolar disorder before starting
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can contribute to dysphagia/aspiration risk, especially in older adults
Photosensitivity: can increase sensitivity to sun exposure
Surgery: manufacturer recommends discontinuation prior to elective surgery due to interaction/arrhythmia risk; discontinuation must be weighed against relapse/discontinuation risks
patient_counseling: If you’re under 25 (or caring for someone who is), take the suicidality warning seriously: monitor mood, agitation, insomnia, irritability, impulsivity, and sudden behavior changes—especially early on and after dose changes.
If you feel intense inner restlessness, stiffness, tremor, or new abnormal movements, contact your prescriber quickly. Don’t “tough it out.”
Go slow when standing up. Dizziness/fainting can happen, and falls are a real risk.
Constipation and urinary retention can become urgent problems—tell your clinician early and manage proactively.
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly reviewed the combo. Sedation and impairment stack.
This medication is not for dementia-related psychosis. In older adults with memory problems, this is usually a ‘no’ unless there’s a very specific reason.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues in real life: sedation, dry mouth/constipation, dizziness from blood pressure drops, and (from perphenazine) movement side effects like restlessness or stiffness.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or a sedated, slowed-down feeling
Constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention (anticholinergic effects)
Dizziness when standing (orthostatic hypotension) and fall risk
Restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, or other EPS
Sexual side effects or hormonal symptoms from prolactin changes (less predictable but possible)

common.patient_note: Many people feel calmer and sleepier early on. That can be helpful for agitation/insomnia, but it can also cause brain fog and daytime impairment—especially during titration.
Dry mouth is common with amitriptyline. It’s annoying, but it also matters medically (teeth/gum issues). Hydration, sugar-free gum/lozenges, and dental care help.
Blood pressure can drop when standing. If you’re getting lightheaded, near-fainting, or falls, that’s a dose-limiting side effect.
Perphenazine can cause movement side effects. Akathisia can feel like unbearable inner agitation and is sometimes mistaken for worsening anxiety—tell your clinician fast.
These can become serious. If you can’t pee, or you go days without a bowel movement with abdominal pain, treat it as urgent.

sections.intro: This combination has meaningful interaction risk. The biggest red flags are MAOIs and anything that adds sedation, anticholinergic burden, or heart rhythm risk.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Don’t stop this medication abruptly unless a clinician tells you to for a safety emergency. Both components can cause rebound and withdrawal-style symptoms. The safer approach is usually a gradual taper, tailored to how long you’ve been on it, your dose, and your symptom history.
key_points: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome can include nausea, dizziness, headaches, sweating/chills, sleep disruption, vivid dreams, anxiety, irritability, and “electric shock” sensations.
Stopping antipsychotics suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms and rebound symptoms: agitation, anxiety, insomnia, GI symptoms, tremor, dyskinesia, and—in some cases—rebound psychosis.
Risk factors for difficult discontinuation: higher dose, longer duration, abrupt stop, and a history of relapse or severe baseline symptoms.
A practical taper is typically stepwise dose reduction over weeks (sometimes longer), slowing down if withdrawal symptoms or relapse signs appear.
If severe EPS, NMS symptoms, severe arrhythmia symptoms, or dangerous confusion develops, seek urgent medical evaluation—those situations can require immediate medication changes under supervision.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing is typically divided across the day (2 to 4 doses). Your prescriber adjusts based on response and tolerability, with a firm ceiling on the daily maximum for both components.

adult.mdd_anxiety_initial: 1 tablet PO 3 to 4 times daily of either amitriptyline 25 mg/perphenazine 2 mg OR amitriptyline 25 mg/perphenazine 4 mg; alternative: 1 tablet (amitriptyline 50 mg/perphenazine 4 mg) PO twice daily
adult.mdd_anxiety_titration: Adjust dose based on response and tolerability; use the smallest effective total daily dose and reassess side effects frequently
adult.mdd_anxiety_max: Maximum daily dose: amitriptyline 200 mg/perphenazine 16 mg per day in 2 to 4 divided doses
adult.predominantly_anxiety_lower_start: If anxiety is predominant, consider lower initial dosing: 1 tablet (amitriptyline 10 mg/perphenazine 4 mg) PO 3 to 4 times daily
adult.schizophrenia_depressive_initial: 2 tablets (amitriptyline 25 mg/perphenazine 4 mg) PO 3 to 4 times daily
adult.schizophrenia_depressive_titration: Adjust dose based on response and tolerability; monitor closely for EPS, orthostasis, sedation, and anticholinergic effects
adult.schizophrenia_depressive_max: Maximum daily dose: amitriptyline 200 mg/perphenazine 16 mg per day in 2 to 4 divided doses
adult.maoi_switching: Allow 14 days between discontinuing an MAOI and starting this medication; allow 14 days between stopping this medication and starting an MAOI
adult.renal_adjustment: Refer to individual agents; use caution in renal impairment and monitor for increased adverse effects
adult.hepatic_adjustment: Use caution; some experts recommend reducing initial and maintenance amitriptyline doses by ~50% in hepatic impairment with cautious adjustments based on response/tolerability; some recommend maximum amitriptyline 100 mg/day in hepatic impairment
adult.older_adult: Avoid use when possible (high-risk in older adults). If used: start low (e.g., 1 tablet amitriptyline 10 mg/perphenazine 4 mg PO 3 to 4 times daily) and titrate cautiously; lower-range dosing is often sufficient in late-onset schizophrenia/psychosis

sections.simple_explanation: This medication is usually dosed multiple times per day. The calming/sedating effect can show up early, while antidepressant benefits often take longer. Because the side-effect burden can be heavy (dry mouth/constipation, dizziness, and movement side effects), dose changes are often limited by tolerability rather than by ambition.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: This medicine is generally avoided in children and often avoided in older adults. Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions are made for each person, through a talk about risks and benefits based on the two individual medicines.
sections.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies did not show harm. Decisions should be based on the risks of each of the two medicines, how severe the illness is, and safer options when available.
sections.lactation: Amitriptyline and perphenazine are present in breast milk. Breastfeeding is not recommended by the manufacturer; if considered, it requires careful clinician oversight and infant monitoring.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for children. Antidepressants carry a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults; this combination is not FDA-approved for children.
sections.geriatrics: Generally avoid. Amitriptyline has strong anticholinergic effects and can cause sedation and orthostatic hypotension. Perphenazine (antipsychotic) is potentially inappropriate in older adults due to stroke risk, cognitive decline, and mortality risk (especially in dementia-related psychosis). Falls, delirium, and hyponatremia risk are key concerns.
sections.hepatic: Use caution because clearance can be reduced and plasma concentrations increased. A conservative approach uses lower initial and maintenance dosing with cautious titration; some expert guidance suggests reducing amitriptyline dosing substantially and keeping the maximum lower in hepatic impairment.
sections.renal: Use caution in renal impairment. Dosing specifics are typically guided by the individual components and by observed tolerability.

Blood chemistries: electrolytes, renal function, liver function, and TSH as clinically indicated

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: In the U.S., this combination is available as oral tablets in multiple fixed-dose strengths.

Tablet (Oral): amitriptyline HCl 10 mg / perphenazine 4 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Amitriptyline increases the synaptic concentration of serotonin and/or norepinephrine in the central nervous system by inhibiting their reuptake. Perphenazine is a piperazine phenothiazine antipsychotic that blocks postsynaptic mesolimbic dopaminergic receptors; it also has alpha-adrenergic blocking effects and influences hypothalamic/pituitary hormone signaling. In plain terms: one part pushes antidepressant signaling, the other part dampens dopamine-driven agitation/psychotic symptoms—together aiming to reduce depression plus agitation/anxiety.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: This is not a modern first-line “default” option for depression or anxiety. It’s a higher-side-effect combination that may be considered when depression is paired with significant anxiety/agitation and a sedating approach is clinically appropriate, or when schizophrenia includes depressive symptoms. The downside is predictable: anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension/falls, cardiac conduction risks, and typical antipsychotic movement side effects. In older adults, it’s usually avoided unless the situation is unusually specific and benefits clearly outweigh harms.

faqs.a: In psychiatry, it’s used for unipolar major depression when anxiety and/or agitation are moderate to severe, and for schizophrenia with depressive symptoms. It’s basically an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic in one tablet—meant for situations where “depression + agitation/anxiety” is the real target.

faqs.q: Is this medication approved for kids or teens?
faqs.a: No. This combination is not approved for children. Antidepressants also carry a boxed warning about a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults, so prescribing for children needs extreme caution and close monitoring – this combination is not a usual choice.

It can help anxiety symptoms that come along with depression—especially when anxiety looks like agitation, insomnia, and feeling keyed-up. It’s not typically used as a standalone anxiety medication, and the side effect burden is heavier than many modern options.

faqs.q: How is it usually dosed for depression with anxiety/agitation?
faqs.a: A common starting approach is 1 tablet three or four times daily of amitriptyline 25 mg/perphenazine 2 mg or 4 mg, or 1 tablet of amitriptyline 50 mg/perphenazine 4 mg twice daily. Doses are adjusted based on response and tolerability, with a maximum daily dose of amitriptyline 200 mg and perphenazine 16 mg in divided doses.

faqs.q: What if my symptoms are mostly anxiety rather than depression?
faqs.a: If anxiety is predominant, lower starting doses may be considered—like 1 tablet of amitriptyline 10 mg/perphenazine 4 mg three to four times daily. The idea is to reduce side effects while still getting a calming effect.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects people notice?
faqs.a: Sleepiness and slowed thinking, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), and movement side effects (stiffness, shaking, and a strong inner restlessness (akathisia)). If you get severe restlessness, new abnormal movements, or you feel faint, do not ignore it – tell your prescriber.

faqs.q: What’s the big boxed warning I should know about?
faqs.a: There are two. (1) Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults (especially early in treatment and with dose changes). Everyone starting an antidepressant should be watched for worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, and unusual changes in behavior. (2) Antipsychotics raise the risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis – this medicine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

faqs.q: Can I take it with an MAOI?
faqs.a: No. You need a washout period. Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting amitriptyline/perphenazine, and allow 14 days between stopping amitriptyline/perphenazine and starting an MAOI.

faqs.q: Why is it usually avoided in older adults?
faqs.a: Because it piles up several risks: strong drying effects (confusion, constipation, trouble peeing), sleepiness, dizziness when standing up and falls, low blood sodium, plus antipsychotic risks (stroke, memory and thinking decline, and a higher risk of death in dementia-related psychosis). For many older adults, the possible harm outweighs the benefit.

faqs.q: How do you stop it safely?
faqs.a: Usually by tapering rather than stopping abruptly—unless there’s a safety emergency. Stopping suddenly can trigger discontinuation symptoms (nausea, dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, irritability) and can also cause rebound symptoms from the antipsychotic side. Taper speed depends on dose, duration, and how your body reacts.

faqs.q: What should I watch for that needs urgent medical attention?
faqs.a: High fever with severe muscle stiffness and confusion (possible NMS), severe fainting, chest pain or palpitations with severe dizziness, inability to urinate, severe constipation with abdominal pain, signs of infection (fever/sore throat) that could signal a blood problem, or rapidly worsening suicidal thoughts—especially early in treatment or after dose changes.
